title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 45
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Keeping People Out
passages.text:
A. A lock does not prevent entry and was never intended to. It delays an intruder, requires them to carry tools or make noise, and leaves evidence that entry was forced, and the security it provides is the sum of those three effects rather than any absolute barrier. Understanding this explains why locks that can be defeated by a determined specialist in minutes remain worth fitting.

B. The oldest designs worked by obstruction and the principle survives in the cheapest modern ones. A bolt held by pins that fall into place under gravity, released by a key shaped to lift each pin to the right height, is an arrangement several thousand years old, and its weakness is that the pins can be manipulated individually by someone who can feel what they are doing. Everything since has been an attempt to prevent that individual manipulation.

C. The trade developed a habit of secrecy that was eventually argued out of it. Makers concealed how their mechanisms worked on the reasoning that an ignorant thief is a less effective one, and were opposed by those who held that concealing a weakness protects the maker rather than the customer, since criminals discover such things anyway and only the owner remains unaware. This argument was conducted in the nineteenth century and its terms are unchanged in current disputes about disclosing software flaws.

D. Mass production changed what a lock had to resist. When each lock was made individually, keys were unique by accident of manufacture; when they were made in quantity, the number of genuinely different key patterns became a specification that could be counted, and a building full of doors might share far fewer combinations than its occupants assumed. Security became a statistical property rather than a craft one.

E. Electronic access solved the key-copying problem and created several others. A credential that can be issued and cancelled remotely, logged, and restricted by time removes most of the administrative weakness of physical keys, and it introduces dependence on power, on a network, and on software that can be attacked from somewhere other than the doorway. The threat moved from the lock to the system behind it.

F. What consistently defeats security is the arrangement around it rather than the mechanism. Doors held open for convenience, keys lent and copied, credentials shared, hinges and frames weaker than the lock, and windows beside the reinforced door account for far more entries than any technical defeat of a mechanism. The lock is usually the strongest part of the arrangement it belongs to, which is why attacking it is rarely necessary.

passages.title: A Mind Built Differently
passages.text:
The octopus is the most substantial test available of whether intelligence must look like ours. Its lineage separated from the vertebrate line before either had anything that could be called a brain, so whatever cognitive capacity it has was arrived at independently, and comparing it with our own is a comparison between two solutions rather than between a solution and a copy.

The architecture is the first surprise. A majority of its neurons are in its arms rather than in its central brain, and an arm removed from central control continues to perform coordinated actions — reaching, gripping, passing objects along — which suggests that a substantial part of the processing happens locally. Whether the animal knows where its arms are in the way we know where our limbs are remains genuinely unresolved.

Behavioural evidence is strong in some areas and weaker than it is usually reported in others. Octopuses solve novel manipulation problems, learn the layout of enclosures, discriminate between individual humans and use objects as shelters and tools by any reasonable definition. Reports of elaborate planning, of play and of long-term memory for events are more variable, and the field has a well-recognised difficulty in that its subjects are individually idiosyncratic and expensive to test in numbers.

Colour is the puzzle that best illustrates the limits of current understanding. Octopuses change skin colour with great precision, matching backgrounds they are apparently unable to see in colour, since their eyes contain a single visual pigment. Explanations have been proposed — light detection in the skin itself, inference from brightness and polarisation — and none is established. A well-defined question about a conspicuous behaviour remains open.

Their lives make the intelligence harder rather than easier to explain. Most species live only one or two years, are solitary, and die shortly after reproducing without contact with their offspring, so there is no opportunity for learning to be passed on and little of the social complexity usually associated with large brains. Whatever selected for these abilities, it was not the pressure of group living or the accumulation of culture.

The uncomfortable implication is ethical rather than scientific. If a capacity resembling intelligence arose twice, independently, on entirely different architecture, then the ability to suffer may also be distributed more widely than convenience suggests, and it cannot be inferred from resemblance to ourselves. Several jurisdictions have extended protections to cephalopods on precisely this reasoning, which is a rare instance of a regulation following an argument rather than a public campaign.

passages.title: Given Away and Everywhere
passages.text:
Almost all significant software runs on components that nobody sold. Operating systems, web servers, databases, encryption libraries and the languages most programs are written in are overwhelmingly available at no cost, modifiable by anyone, and maintained outside any single company — an arrangement that ought to be unstable and has instead become the foundation of the industry.

Why anyone contributes has a duller answer than the early accounts suggested. Some contribution is genuinely voluntary, but the majority of work on major projects is now done by people paid by companies that depend on the software, which is a rational investment rather than a gift: a firm whose product runs on a component wants that component maintained, and paying an engineer to work on it is cheaper than maintaining a private version. The commons is funded by the people who need it to keep working.

The failure mode is a specific and well-documented one. Some critical components are maintained by very small numbers of unpaid people, and the demands on them scale with adoption while nothing else does — security reports, compatibility requests, and pressure from organisations that pay nothing and expect responsiveness. Serious vulnerabilities have been found in software running on an enormous fraction of the world's systems and maintained, at the time, by one or two individuals in their own time.

Licences do a great deal of work that is easy to overlook. A licence permitting anything at all encourages the widest use and permits a company to take the code, improve it privately and release nothing; a licence requiring modifications to be shared keeps improvements in the commons and deters some commercial adoption. Both models have produced successful projects, and the choice between them is a strategic decision about which failure a project would rather have.

The business models built on this are less varied than they appear. Selling support and operational hosting for software that is free to acquire, keeping some features proprietary while giving away a core, and selling a managed service that removes the difficulty of running it yourself are broadly the options. The tension in all of them is that the better a company makes the free version, the less anyone needs the paid one.

The security argument has been settled in a direction neither side expected. Openness does not by itself produce scrutiny — code that nobody reads is not safer for being readable — but it makes scrutiny possible, and the widely used projects with funded review are among the most examined software in existence. Obscurity in commercial code prevents neither attackers nor discovery, and the distinguishing factor turned out to be whether anyone is actually paid to look.
